messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 75
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Potter
- Trauma Type: Refugee
- Pcl5: 50

He is seventy-five now, a South Asian man with hands still shaped by clay. When he speaks about his life, he often begins with the wheel. As a boy, he learns from his father how to center wet earth with steady pressure, how to keep a vessel from collapsing by not forcing it too fast. Before the war and the flight, there is rhythm: the courtyard, the kiln, his mother calling from the kitchen, customers arriving before festivals to order water jars and lamps. He marries young. By the time violence reaches his town, he is already a husband, already a potter in his own right, with a small workshop and shelves lined with bowls drying in the heat.

At first, the danger comes as rumor. Neighbors lower their voices. Shops close early. Men gather at corners and stop talking when others approach. Then it becomes visible. Armed men move through nearby streets. Houses are marked. One evening he hears shouting, then the crack of gunfire so close that the windows rattle. He remembers his wife clutching their child against her chest and looking at him as if he should know what to do. The next days blur into terror and waiting. Smoke rises from a part of town where relatives live. A cousin arrives breathless and ash-streaked, saying they must leave now, with only what they can carry.

He still sees the moment they abandon the workshop. The clay on the wheel is half-shaped, one wall of a vessel thinner than the other. He covers it out of habit, as though he might return that evening. Instead he locks the door with trembling hands and joins the stream of people leaving. The road out is crowded and chaotic. Children cry from hunger and fear. At checkpoints he keeps his eyes down, afraid that one wrong glance will bring attention to his family. He remembers bodies by the roadside, remembers the sickly smell in the heat, remembers trying not to let his son look. He does not speak much about the crossing itself; when he gets near that part of the story, his breathing grows shallow and he stares past the room, as if seeing again the river, the pushing crowd, the panic when they are separated for several minutes that feel to him like an entire lifetime.

In the refugee camp, he becomes a man who waits. He waits for food, for documents, for news, for permission, for morning. The shame of that period stays with him. He has always worked with his hands, always made things people need, and now he stands in lines feeling useless. He tells himself his family survived and that should be enough, yet he cannot stop scanning faces, counting heads, making sure his wife and child are still there. At night he jerks awake drenched in sweat, convinced he has heard boots outside the tent. If someone coughs or cries out nearby, his heart slams so hard he presses a palm to his chest. Sleep becomes thin and unreliable.

Years later, after resettlement, he returns to pottery in a small way. He works steadily, eventually building a modest reputation in his community for strong, elegant household pieces. Customers know him as quiet, dependable, meticulous. They do not see how easily he startles when a truck backfires outside the studio, how his shoulders rise and remain tense for hours after. When clay collapses on the wheel, he can become abruptly irritable, cursing under his breath, then ashamed of his own anger. His wife has learned not to wake him suddenly. If she touches his shoulder when he is asleep in the chair, he sometimes swings an arm before he is fully conscious, then looks at her with horror.

He avoids crowds whenever he can. Weddings, markets, religious festivals—once sources of belonging—now exhaust him. He positions himself near exits and keeps watch over grandchildren so closely that his family teases him, though not unkindly. He laughs with them, but he does not relax. News footage of displaced families pulls him in and overwhelms him at once. He cannot turn away, yet afterward he is withdrawn for the rest of the day, moving around the house as if carrying something heavy and invisible.

He says the past comes back most strongly in ordinary moments. The smell of smoke from a neighbor’s yard can transport him before he understands why his hands are shaking. Seeing rows of shoes outside a prayer hall can suddenly remind him of the camp. Sometimes while kneading clay he is overtaken by the memory of packing in haste, of choosing what to carry and what to leave, and he feels again the unbearable knowledge that a whole life can be abandoned in minutes. He tells himself he is safe, that he is an old man in his own workshop, that his wife is in the next room making tea. Still, he checks the locks each night more than once. Still, he dreams of running with his family through smoke. Still, part of him remains on that road, listening for danger, unable to believe that survival and safety are the same thing.
